user: California tells me I didn't file documents for an LLC that isn't mine. What do I do?
assistant: The California Department of State handles the business entities registration. I would recommend the following steps:
1. Visit the California Secretary of State's website and look up the LLC in question. SOS is Secretary of State. SOS number is the number the Secretary of State office assigned to your entity. This will provide you with information about the LLC, including its founders and public records.
2. Obtain the registered agent's name and address for the LLC. You can then use this information to contact them and ask why your address is listed as the LLC's business address.
3. Contact the Secretary of State and inform them that you are not associated with the LLC. 
It's important to gather as much information as you can before contacting the state to ensure that you have the best answers possible. Answering "I don't know" won't be as helpful as providing detailed and informed responses.

user: What is an LLC for?
assistant: An LLC, or Limited Liability Company, is a type of business structure that combines the pass-through taxation of a partnership or sole proprietorship with the limited liability of a corporation. This means that if there is any chance of liability, you should protect yourself with an LLC. Then it is much more difficult for them to sue and take personal assets, debts and judgments against your business can put your personal assets at risk!
user: How do I set up an LLC?
assistant: Start by asking an accountant and/or a lawyer if an LLC is what you need. The LLC can be formed within just 24 hrs from the time of submitting of the form. The LLC filing itself in most cases is a simple fill in the blank form. You can likely file yourself either online or through the mail, depending on the state. Use a service if you're not sure what to do to ensure it is correct.
user: Do I need a license for an LLC?
assistant: The need for a specific business license for an LLC depends on the type of business and the state in which it operates. It's advisable to check with your local Secretary of State's office or a business licensing service to determine if a license is required for your LLC. However, if the compliance kit of the service you're considering involves business licensing research, it may be worthwhile. You can also order those services a la carte from vendors like LLX and BusinessLicenses.com.
[The End of Previous Conversation]

[The Start of Current Turn Question]
Sole proprietorship or S-Corp, what should I do?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
The choice between a sole proprietorship and an S-Corp depends on various factors, including the nature of your business, your liability exposure, and your tax situation. There are a lot of options with a sole proprietorship being the easiest to manage, with minimal formalities and regulations. The main disadvantages of an S-Corporation or an LLC are that it adds a lot of management overhead (time, and possibly money if you don't do it all yourself), and there are fees you must pay to incorporate, as well as additional yearly maintenance fees which vary by state. You should be able to weigh the tax savings and liability protection against the extra costs and hassle. However, setting up and maintaining an S-Corp is more complex. It is recommended to consult with a legal or financial professional to help determine the best option for your specific situation.
[The End of Reference Answer]

[The Start of Assistant's Answer]
The documents don’t establish which is best for you. They suggest weighing potential tax savings and liability protection against added management work, incorporation fees, and annual maintenance fees, which vary by state. As a rule of thumb, an S-Corp becomes more attractive as your business or income grows. [S2]

Location also matters: the document says that in NYC, an S-Corp could result in slightly higher taxes than a sole proprietorship. [S3]

What state and city will you operate in, what annual business income do you expect, and how important is liability protection to you? Without those details, I can’t determine which option the documents favor for your situation.
[The End of Assistant's Answer]

[The Start of Document]
  It's a state-level organization. Your LLC can elect to be treated as a partnership, a disregarded entity (i.e., just report the taxes in your individual income tax), or as an S-Corp for federal tax purposes. If you have elected S-Corp, I expect that all the S-Corp rules will apply, as well as any state-level LLC rules that may apply.   Disclaimer: I'm not 100% familiar with S-corp rules, so I can't evaluate whether the statements you made about proportional payouts are correct.

Compared with a Sole Proprietorship, the main disadvantages of an S-Corporation or an LLC are that it adds a lot of management overhead (time, and possibly money if you don't do it all yourself), and there are fees you must pay to incorporate, as well as additional yearly maintenance fees which vary by state. You should be able to weigh the tax savings and liability protection against the extra costs and hassle, and see which way the scales tip. As a rule of thumb, the bigger your business gets or the more income you make, the more attractive incorporating becomes.

 For example, IL and CA charge 1.5% tax, NY is less, but NYC is 8.85%! In NYC specifically, you could actually end up paying slightly more tax as an S-Corp than you would as a Sole Proprietorship. In most places though, the nominal local taxes will still be less than the FICA taxes you could potentially save.

  The 50/50 split thing should be in writing along with a bunch of other issues. You could have one of you doing a sole proprietorship where the other person is a contractor that receives half of all revenues/profits.  The person that owns the sole proprietorship may be entitled to deduct certain costs of running the entity.  The other person would then be 1099'd his share of revenues.

 You could also setup an LLC that is organized as any of the above.  I would only do this if you can self fund some additional tax preparation costs.  Figure about $600/year at a minimum.
[The End of Document]
